newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-Capital to open new Radio Cafes.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Capital to open new Radio Cafes.

text.p: Britain's Capital Radio Plc plans to open new Radio Cafes as part of its development into a broader music entertainment company, new chief executive David Mansfield said on Friday.

Mansfield, who will succeed Richard Eyre as chief executive, told Reuters the group also saw significant scope for margin improvement and cost reduction at its recently-acquired My Kinda Town restaurant operation.
Capital plans to expand the Radio Cafe format with venues around London and in Birmingham in central England and Southampton on the south coast.
Mansfield said Capital was in talks over sites in Birmingham and Southampton, areas where it has commercial radio operations.
It is also seeking locations south of the capital at Kingston, Croydon and Guildford, within range of its flagship London FM radio station, with a view to opening cafes.
Capital opened its first Radio Cafe last November at its headquarters in Leicester Square, central London. It also paid 51 million stg for the My Kinda Town chain of bars and themed diners.
Mansfield said he and newly appointed My Kinda Town chief executive Russell Scott were looking at ways of boosting margins.

"We are looking very closely at the cost base. There is room for some significant improvements in margins," he said, adding head office and administration costs, particularly of overseas operations, would be examined.
My Kinda Town operates more than 50 outlets in 16 countries. Mansfield said that some of its brands were nearing the end of their life cycle.

He noted the group's Latin American venues in London were performing well and said other sites in London and Birmingham could be converted to this style. One of the advantages is that these venues charge admission fees.
Capital shares fell a further 9p on Friday to trade at 506p, hovering around their lowest levels for a year.
Analysts said the departure of Eyre, who is to become ITV chief executive after six years at Capital, was hurting sentiment.

"It's disappointing that he's not around to see through the expansion strategy he started," said Anthony de Larrinaga of Panmure Gordon. He added that worries about prospects for advertising revenue and consumer spending next year were also clouding the outlook.
Capital is awaiting regulatory clearance for its acquisition of Richard Branson's Virgin Radio.
The deal, if approved, would give the enlarged group a guaranteed national digital broadcast licence, which becomes available in 1998.
Mansfield said digital, which will offer CD-quality sound to owners of new digital receivers, would transform AM services like Virgin's national rock station.
"The big advantage of digital is the improvement to AM services. Music and AM are just not a winning combination," he said.
